title: The quarrel of the senses
hookLine: speech, eye, ear and mind each claim to be the best, until the breath begins to leave
carry: prana: breath is life, chief of the senses
tomorrow: Why does the god raise an open palm?

lines: SPEECH, EYE, EAR, MIND: I AM THE BEST.
cards: Long ago, an Upanishad says, the powers of a person had an argument. Speech, the eye, the ear and the mind each said: I am the best. They went to Prajapati, the creator, to settle it.
He told them, in paraphrase: the one whose leaving makes the body worst off, that one is the best. So, one by one, they left. Speech went first, and stayed away for a whole year.

teach.h: THE BODY LIVES ON WITHOUT EACH.
teach.b: When speech came back, it asked how the body had managed. In paraphrase: like someone who can't speak, but still breathing, seeing, hearing, thinking. Then the eye left for a year, and the body lived on like the blind.
Then the ear, and it lived on like the deaf. Then the mind, and it lived on like a small child.

teach.h: THEN THE BREATH BEGINS TO LEAVE.
teach.b: Then the breath began to leave. And the Chandogya Upanishad gives it a picture: like a strong horse tearing up the pegs it was tied to, the breath started tearing all the others up with it.
They cried out together, in paraphrase: stay, lord, you are the best of us. That's the teaching.

teach.h: STAY, LORD. PRANA IS LIFE ITSELF.
teach.b: In Hindu thought, breath is prana, life itself, the chief of all the powers, treated as sacred.
The Hatha Yoga Pradipika describes alternate-nostril breathing, in paraphrase: in through the left, out through the right; in through the right, out through the left.
It says this is how the nadis, the channels of the subtle body, are made clean. The text's version also holds the breath, which teachers say to learn in person.

teach.h: VISHNU MUDRA: ONE NOSTRIL, THEN THE OTHER.
teach.b: Teachers supply the hand: in some lineages, Vishnu mudra, two fingers folded down, the thumb and ring finger free to close each side in turn.
Many who say the daily sandhya prayers begin with pranayama, the right hand at the nose. An app may call this a stress hack.
But in the Upanishad's story, breath isn't a tool you use. It's the one that, when it starts to leave, everything else begs to stay.

how: In hatha yoga and before the daily sandhya prayers, many Hindus do alternate-nostril breathing with the right hand, folding the first two fingers and closing each side in turn; breath retention is learned from a teacher.

games.q: the chief of the senses — tap the pairs.
p: left first, for a whole year
tore the others up like a horse its pegs

s: in the Upanishad's story, the body dies when speech leaves
it lives on like someone who can't speak, still breathing, seeing and thinking.
when the breath starts to leave, the other powers beg it to stay
they call it lord, and the best of them.
the Hatha Yoga Pradipika spells out the hand shape for this breathing
the passage describes the breath, left and right; teachers supply the hand shape.

games.q: you're Prajapati. speech, eye, ear and mind each say they're the best. how do you settle it?
o: the one whose leaving hurts the body most is the best.
give the prize to the loudest.
games.why: Prajapati says the best is the one whose leaving leaves the body worst off. Only the breath's leaving threatens them all.

practice: Sit upright and fold the first two fingers of the right hand into the palm.

Close the right nostril with the thumb and breathe in through the left; close the left with the ring finger and breathe out through the right; breathe in through the right, then switch and breathe out through the left: one round.

Slow and easy, no holding, no forcing. If you pray, let a name of God ride on each breath; if not, just count the rounds. If the nose is blocked or anything feels uncomfortable, rest the hand and breathe normally.

wordCard.voice: The mudras. Today, the breathing hand: two fingers folded, thumb and ring finger tending prana, the breath the Upanishad calls chief of all.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: prana, breath, life. In the Upanishad's story, the chief of all the powers.
